{{Please leave this line alone (sandbox heading)}} {{Infobox television episode | title = Pingu's Dream | series = [[Pingu]] | image = | caption = | season = 1 (purported) | episode = Unnumbered (withdrawn) | director = Uncredited | writer = Unknown | airdate = {{Start date|1981|05|12}} (withdrawn) | chronicler = | guests = | prev = | next = }} "'''Pingu's Dream'''" (originally referred to in internal production notes as '''''Pingu und der schattenhafte Besucher''''') is a purported, unnumbered television pilot or test short associated with the Swiss stop-motion claymation series ''[[Pingu]]''. While the official series pilot was created by [[Otmar Gutmann]] in 1986 and debuted on television in 1990, "Pingu's Dream" reportedly aired a single time on Swiss public broadcaster [[SRG SSR]] on 12 May 1981 before being immediately pulled and erased from broadcasting schedules. The episode is famous within television history and [[lost media]] circles because Otmar Gutmann, the credited creator of the franchise, explicitly denied any knowledge of its production, script, or broadcast until his death in 1993.Mazzola, Silvio (1995). *Claymation and Compromise: The Early Years of Trickfilmstudio*. Zurich: Tele-Press. == Premise and Content == According to contemporary viewers and surviving broadcast logs, the short was roughly seven minutes long and differed dramatically from the playful, lighthearted tone of the later established series. The episode begins normally, with Pingu playing outside his family's igloo. However, the atmosphere shifts as the sun suddenly drops below the horizon, plunging the landscape into complete darkness. Pingu retreats inside to his bed, where the episode transitions into a highly surreal, experimental nightmare sequence: * '''The Shadow Visitor:''' Unlike the iconic giant walrus from the official Season 1 episode "Pingu's Dream" (1990), this short featured a completely black, non-reflective silhouette of a towering, elongated penguin figure that casting a static shadow directly against the wind. * '''Audio Deviations:''' The character of Pingu did not speak in his signature "Pinguinese" gibberish (voiced by [[Carlo Bonomi]]). Instead, the character remained entirely silent, while the background track consisted of a low-frequency, looping metallic scraping noise accompanied by a rhythmic, heavy heartbeat. The episode ended abruptly with Pingu staring directly into the camera lens as his clay face slowly flattened out, cutting to a harsh black screen with no production credits. == Production Inconsistency == The episode's existence presents a major chronological anomaly in the timeline of Trickfilmstudio (the production house behind ''Pingu''). In 1981, Otmar Gutmann was primarily working on short, independent animation experiments and commercial work, and had not yet finalized the character designs or intellectual property rights for the ''Pingu'' universe. During an interview with German animation magazine ''Animatasia'' in 1991, Gutmann was asked about the legendary "1981 incident." He responded:
"I have seen the logs, and I have heard the rumors, but I did not make this. In 1981, Pingu did not exist outside of my personal sketchbook. Whoever put that clay on a stage in Zurich did so without my hands, my studio, or my permission."Gutmann, Otmar (November 1991). "On Clay and Penguins". *Animatasia Magazine* (Interview). Interviewed by Karl-Heinz Dörner.
Media historians hypothesize that the short may have been an unauthorized overnight project executed by a rogue technician or apprentice at the Swiss studio using early prototype armatures, which accidentally bypassed scheduling filters and entered the live automated broadcast loop.Mazzola, Silvio (1995). == Public Reaction and Suppression == The lone broadcast occurred during a mid-afternoon children's programming block on 12 May 1981. Within minutes of the broadcast concluding, the station's switchboard was overwhelmed by hundreds of calls from distressed parents reporting that their toddlers had broken into fits of crying or refused to sleep in their bedrooms. The network immediately issued an on-air apology, scrubbed the master log index entry, and replaced all scheduled morning re-runs with classic episodes of ''[[The Linea]]''. The master tape of the episode was reportedly marked for physical disposal to prevent further corporate liability. == Lost Media Status == Because the broadcast occurred long before the widespread consumer adoption of home recording devices like [[VHS]] in Switzerland, no authentic off-air recordings have ever emerged. In 2018, a private collector claimed to have found a 35mm magnetic audio reel containing the isolated sound design of the episode, but the authenticity of the track remains heavily disputed by archivists. == See also == * [[Pingu]] * [[Lost media]] * [[Uncanny valley]] == References == {{Reflist}} [[Category:Pingu episodes]] [[Category:Lost television episodes]] [[Category:Banned television programmes]] [[Category:1981 television episodes]]
